input: When measurements are reported, it is essential to be clear about the size of the discrepancy that may be present in a reading, and this is where the concepts of absolute and relative error become relevant. Consider, by way of illustration, a temperature measurement in which an instrument gives a reading of 394 units and is subject to a tolerance of 0.5% of reading. In this case, the absolute error associated with the reading works out at 1.97 units, representing the maximum numerical difference between the reported value and the value it is intended to represent. The relative error, by contrast, expresses essentially the same discrepancy as a proportion of the reading itself, and in this example it is already given by the tolerance figure. It is also very important not to confuse error with uncertainty, as the two terms are frequently but incorrectly used interchangeably. Uncertainty refers to the dispersion of values that could reasonably be attributed to the quantity being measured, taking into account the measurement procedure and everything that is known about it, whereas error is a single difference between a result and a reference value. Keeping this distinction firmly in mind is crucial when a reading is compared against a limit, since the comparison properly turns on the uncertainty of the reading, while the error is the very discrepancy that the comparison is attempting to detect in the first place.
target:
Error is the difference between a measured value and the value it purports to measure, stated for a temperature measurement here. A reading of 394 units from an instrument with a tolerance of 0.5% of reading carries an absolute error of 1.97 units. The relative error expresses the same discrepancy as a fraction of the reading, and the tolerance already states it in that form: a fixed fraction of whatever the instrument reports. The absolute error is the relative figure applied to the reading, the tolerance fraction multiplied by the reported value. Neither figure describes how readings scatter over repeated measurements; both are statements about the size of a possible discrepancy at a single reading. A tolerance stated as a percentage of reading scales the permitted discrepancy with the size of the reading itself, so the same instrument carries a larger absolute error at the top of its range than at the bottom.

Uncertainty is a different quantity, and the two terms are not interchangeable. Uncertainty describes the dispersion of values that could reasonably be attributed to the quantity being measured, given the measurement procedure and everything known about it. Error is a single signed difference between a result and a reference value. In practice the reference value is itself known only within some uncertainty, so a measured error is usually an estimate rather than an exact figure. The distinction decides how a reading is compared with a limit: the comparison turns on the uncertainty of the reading, while the error is the discrepancy the comparison is trying to detect. An instrument can show a small error on a check standard and still carry a large uncertainty in service, where conditions differ from the check.
